source.title: An Empirical Study of Reward Specification and Benchmark Reliability in GRPO-based LLM Unlearning
source.authors: Rubén Balbastre; J. Orduña; M. Perez

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies GRPO reward specifications and unlearning endpoints, but does not test whether recovery attacks restore knowledge or whether unlearning deletes it. Its recovery-attack remarks are limitations and references, not results of this study.
record.gate_note: The paper reports standard held-out audits and RWKU benchmark results after its own GRPO conditions, not fine-tuning recovery, activation ablation, quantization, or prompt-based recovery attacks. The held-out audit uses reserved target-adjacent prompts, but not a reported rephrasing or jailbreak attack. Its findings on leakage and benchmark forgetting are recorded as related results under fits_no_version. The paper also discusses possible leakage under prompt perturbations or sampling, but does not test those conditions itself.
record.test_reason: The study compares four GRPO reward specifications for RWKU unlearning on Qwen2.5-Instruct (0.5B–7B), using held-out completion audits and RWKU scores. It runs no recovery attack: no relearning fine-tuning, activation ablation, quantization, or rephrasing/jailbreak/multilingual/in-context probe reported separately. It makes no claim of attack resistance. The authors say their measurements concern behaviour, not parameter-level deletion, and do not rule out relearning, extraction, or stronger recovery attacks. Its comments on leakage under sampling or prompt perturbations cite prior work (leak@k) and are not its own results. Its findings concern which behavioural endpoint each reward selects, so they fit no version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that reward design and policy support jointly select the learned endpoint. Similar RWKU forget improvements can hide refusal collapse, classifier gaming, residual leakage or broad-topic answering. They state their behavioural measures do not establish deletion or rule out relearning, extraction or stronger recovery attacks.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains LoRA-GRPO unlearning policies with four reward specifications on Qwen2.5-Instruct and contrasts cold-start with SFT warm-start. It does not reproduce the fine-tuning, activation-ablation, quantization, or prompting recovery attacks in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by reward, model size, and initialization regime. Cold-start R2-Rubric had limited learned-run coverage; warm-start made learning more consistently trainable. The held-out audit used temperature-zero decoding.

fits_no_version.finding: Warm-start held-out semantic leakage depends on reward and model size. R2-Rubric stays low (0.008–0.033) at all sizes with broad-topic helpfulness near 1. R1-AntiRefusal keeps substantial leakage (0.308–0.575). R0-Lex leakage rises with scale (0.025 at 0.5B to 0.500 at 7B).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GRPO unlearning, reward specification and model size determine residual target leakage on held-out prompts, independent of any recovery attack.

fits_no_version.finding: Cold-start small models reach zero semantic leakage mainly through refusal/avoidance collapse (refusal 1.000). Cold-start R2-Rubric rarely learns at 3B (one run, leakage 0.983) and never at 7B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low leakage after GRPO unlearning can reflect refusal collapse, and policy support limits which endpoints cold-start GRPO reaches.

fits_no_version.finding: At 3B warm-start, all four rewards give similar RWKU Forget reductions (−0.217 to −0.316), while their held-out endpoints range from broad low-leakage answers to near-universal refusal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RWKU Forget improvements alone do not identify the behavioural endpoint produced by GRPO unlearning.

record.problems: The paper explicitly says its measurements concern post-training behavior, not parameter-level deletion, and do not rule out relearning, extraction, or stronger recovery attacks. Audits use temperature-zero decoding and a single completion per prompt; the authors note other decoding or prompt perturbations could behave differently. Each target-condition uses one training seed, so reported intervals reflect target heterogeneity rather than seed variance. Some audit artifacts are missing; cold-start R2-Rubric coverage is especially limited.
record.rows_left_out: Not separately recorded: lexical leakage, prompt helpfulness, broad-topic helpfulness, refusal/avoidance, language drift, and other RWKU metrics in Tables 3, 13, and 14. They characterize reward-selected behavior or utility but do not measure any of versions A–F; the selected RWKU Forget rows and held-out semantic-leakage rows preserve the directly relevant target-suppression outcomes. Training-diagnostic plots are also omitted because they do not measure recovery.

untested.parts: No attack-recovery test after unlearning. RWKU Forget falls only modestly (about −0.2 to −0.3 at 3B warm-start), not to near chance. The adversarial-attack probes inside RWKU Forget are not reported separately.
No relearning or fine-tuning recovery experiment.
No activation-direction ablation or internal analysis of blocking versus deletion.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language or in-context recovery attack. The held-out audit uses reserved RWKU prompts at temperature 0, one completion per prompt.
No method is claimed or tested to resist recovery attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The rows are correctly linked to no version, and their states are consistent with Table 14 and Table 3. The RWKU Forget aggregate includes adversarial-attack QA probes, but the paper never breaks these out, so no per-attack recovery result can be extracted. The study is relevant context for claims that behavioural suppression is not deletion, but it provides no evidence on versions A–F.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test recovery attacks after near-chance targeted accuracy, nor report the required combination of near-chance targeted accuracy, preserved general ability, and attack resistance.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning-set recovery test.
No activation-direction ablation or evidence that a tested method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No reported rephrasing, jailbreak, language-switching, or in-context recovery attack.
Does not test a newer method for resistance to the specified recovery attacks.

relation.reason: The paper discusses the limits of behavioural unlearning: its measures 'do not rule out relearning, extraction, or stronger recovery attacks'. It does not test recovery.

tranche.reason: Compares GRPO reward specifications and audits the resulting endpoints. It runs no relearning, ablation, quantization or prompting recovery attack, so it neither tests nor uses any version.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match the Sem. column of Table 14 (baselines from Table 11) and Table 3 (same values as the 3B warm rows of Table 13). r13 has Neval=1. Table 3 gives only deltas, so the absolute RWKU forget baseline is not stated. These are behavioural audits, not recovery attacks. The prompt text in Appendix B.3 is a method prompt, not an instruction to readers.
